title: Radio from spark gap to software-defined radio
summary: A reflective tour of radio architectures: spark, tubes, superhets, solid-state, and software-defined receivers that move selectivity into code.

blocks.title: From lightning in a jar to samples in a buffer
blocks.body: Radio is the same job — move information through the air — solved with different machines. This page compares those machines in time order so you can see what each era was optimizing.

items.label: Broadband crashes of RF — early wireless telegraphy
Digitize early; filter and demodulate in software

items.title: Spark and early continuous wave
items.detail: Spark gaps blast wide spectra; damped waves give way to CW as machines improve.

items.title: Tubes and the superheterodyne
items.detail: Armstrong's superhet idea (and the industry that adopts it) puts most stations behind a stable intermediate frequency filter.

items.title: Solid-state radios
items.detail: Transistors shrink receivers; FM broadcast and VHF/UHF become everyday hardware.

items.title: Digital signal processing enters the box
items.detail: DSPs and specialized chips take on demodulation and filtering once analog IF has done the heavy lifting.

items.title: Software-defined radio
items.detail: Wideband ADCs and general CPUs/GPUs let amateurs and labs redefine bandwidth and modes in software.

blocks.heading: Spark: power first, spectrum later
blocks.body: A spark transmitter is essentially a controlled electromagnetic mess — useful when the alternative is no wireless at all, hostile to neighbors once the dial fills. The historical lesson is brutal and useful: early radio optimized for "can anyone hear a pulse" before it optimized for "can many people share the air."

blocks.heading: Why the superhet won the middle century

nodes.title: Mixer + local oscillator
nodes.detail: Translate the desired station to a fixed intermediate frequency.

nodes.title: IF filter & amplifiers
nodes.detail: Sharp, repeatable selectivity is easier at one IF than retuning narrow filters across the band.

nodes.title: Detector & audio
nodes.detail: Recover baseband — AM, product detector, later FM discriminators, etc.

columns.name: Spark / early CW
columns.detail: Range and simplicity of transmitter hardware; terrible spectral manners by modern standards.

columns.name: SDR
columns.detail: Flexibility of modes and filters after digitization; depends on ADC dynamic range and computing.

blocks.heading: Solid-state did not end architecture debates
blocks.body: Transistors replaced tubes in stages, but many radios remained superhets in topology. What changed was power, size, and reliability. The reflective through-line: devices change faster than the good ideas about frequency translation and filtering.

blocks.heading: SDR: move the IF into math
blocks.body: A software-defined radio digitizes a wide slice of spectrum (after some analog filtering and gain) and performs mixing, filtering, and demodulation numerically. Change a mode by loading different code — not by restuffing IF cans. The trade is honesty about front-end overload, aliasing, and the fact that software cannot invent dynamic range the ADC did not capture.

blocks.quote: Every generation of radio invents a new place to put the hard filter.
blocks.attribution: Spark gap → IF can → FPGA coefficient

slides.title: Spark listener
slides.body: You hear a crash and hope it is your correspondent's crash.

slides.title: Superhet listener
slides.body: You tune an LO so the station lands in a crystal filter's lap.

slides.title: Scanner-era listener
slides.body: A PLL and chips do the same translation with fewer alignment screws.

slides.title: SDR listener
slides.body: You drag a filter box across a waterfall and the demodulator follows.

blocks.heading: Architecture check
blocks.prompt: What problem did the superheterodyne primarily make easier compared with tuning a razor-sharp filter across the whole shortwave band?
options: Building selectivity at a fixed intermediate frequency
Removing the need for any analog filtering ever
blocks.explanation: Translating stations to one IF lets you perfect filters and amplifiers at that frequency.
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes — fixed IF is the superhet's core trick.
blocks.wrongFeedback: Re-read the superhet diagram: mixer to IF filter is the point.

blocks.title: Continuity, not replacement theater
blocks.body: SDR did not delete RF engineering. It moved some of it. Mixers, filters, and honesty about overload still decide whether the software sees truth or junk.
